chapter_theme: Paripadal 8, to Sevvel at Parankundram: the thirty-three gods take refuge in him and the hill equals the Himalaya of his birth; the rains, creatures and flowers make his procession to Koodal; the hill's fame is unending love; a wife forbids her guilty husband to swear by Murugan and turns her grief to worship; the festival crowd's offerings and petitions; bathing lovers at the pool, and a prayer that the hill's waters outlast the rain.

paripadal:8:1-16.reading: The poet lists the gods who have come to cling to Murugan as their refuge: Thirumal of the bird banner and blooming tulasi, the rider of the bull, the first one on the lotus, the twelve who drive darkness from the world, the two who speak of medicine, the eight of the ordered texts, the eleven lords named from the lord of Aathirai, the guardians of the quarters, gods, asuras and the great ascetics; because of him Parankundram equals the Himalaya, and the pool of his hill, where falls hang like garlands, equals the one still pool of the Himalaya where the ranked lotus that bore him blooms in flashing clusters.
paripadal:8:1-16.nuance: Lines 4 to 7 count the Vedic thirty-three by their groups (10 and 2, 2, 8, 11), so the hill is made the meeting place of the whole older pantheon. The argument of lines 11 to 16 is a transfer of sanctity: the Pandya hill equals the Himalaya because its pool equals the pool of his birth. மாலைச் சுனை (line 16) can be the garland-like pool of the falls or the pool at evening.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god through the gods who serve him and the hill that equals his birthplace, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the falls hanging into the pool

paripadal:8:17-28.reading: The rain cloud's voice answers like one that has heard the trumpeting of the god's elephant; hearing it the cocks crow till the hill shakes, the musth elephants trumpet back and the caves return the echo; bees of every kind hum like the music of seven-holed and five-holed instruments, the pools bloom, the konrai lets down its clusters, the creepers flower for weddings, the kanthal opens its mouth, honey drips and the south breeze stirs, and this, the poet says, is the splendour of the coming from your hill to Koodal.
paripadal:8:17-28.nuance: The unit is a chain of answering sounds (elephant, cloud, cock, elephant, cave) that turns into a chain of opening flowers; the god's presence is heard before it is seen. கூடல் வரவு (line 28) makes the scene a procession from the hill to the Pandya city, not only a landscape.

thinai_evidence.note: the season and the hill's creatures praised as the god's own procession, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the rain cloud

comparisons.vehicle: ஏழ் புழை ஐம் புழை யாழ் இசை
comparisons.tenor: the hum of the swarming bees

paripadal:8:29-46.reading: Hailing the god whose shining spear split the mountain, the poet says that when the wedding drums of Koodal roar, the hill answers back and forth like the wind-churned sea, like the cloud drinking the ocean, like Indra's thunder, and its answer is a proclamation: the humming of the bee swarms, the lovers' messengers, rings over the walls of their old town; women with eyes finer than cut mango, bodies like mango shoots, bamboo shoulders and small bangles find on the grove beds of the hill a desire that is never sated, an enjoyment that does not end, a love never complete, and the young men's union, unparting like the makanril pair on spread flowers, is a joy that never fades; such is the fame of cool Parankundram, which gives without forgetting.
paripadal:8:29-46.nuance: The hill's fame is stated as erotic, not ascetic: the god's hill is praised as the place where love never reaches its end (ஆராக் காமம், வரையா நுகர்ச்சி, முடியா நுகர்ச்சி, முற்றாக் காதல்), a string of negated limits that matches the praise of the god's own boundlessness. The makanril, the water bird proverbial for never leaving its mate, is here part of a comparison of the young men's union, not a separate carrier, so it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill praised by the love it grants: paadaan carrying akam matter

comparisons.tenor: the young men's union with the women

paripadal:8:47-71.reading: A wife accuses her husband: he smells of strangers, has played on the hill with dewy-eyed women and comes back smiling evening after evening, gone at morning and home at night, so let him stop swearing by the hill; he answers that the scent is only the wind off the Vaigai groves and the dewy slopes, and begs her not to sulk; she cuts him off, calls him the unworthy son of worthy parents, mimics the oath he will offer (I touched the Vaigai's sand, I touched the foot of the hill of the god who grants marriage), and forbids him to swear by Murugan, by the peacock and the shadow of the spear, by the feet of holy men or by the hunter's daughter, since the true spear of that god would devour him; if he must swear, let him swear by the hill and the sand of the Vaigai.
paripadal:8:47-71.nuance: Her refusal is protective as much as scornful: she does not doubt that the god enforces an oath (அணங்கான் மெய் வேல் தின்னும், line 66), she doubts the man, and so she steers him to an oath by sand, which cannot strike him. குறவன் மகள் (line 69) is Valli, already a name to swear by. The speaker of lines 51 to 55 is not marked, and the turns between wife and husband are a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulking at a husband who smells of other women and offers oaths: the oodal of marutham

paripadal:8:72-89.reading: The quarrel goes on (who left, who came, who asked, who told?): he says she calls his oath worthless and praises her neythal eyes, bud-like smile, honeyed lips, bright brow and teeth whiter than jasmine buds and like pearls, saying what he speaks is neither dream nor waking; she says the anger she has taken on will not cool and her grief grows, and turns to the god: let us go to his feet, offer flowers, feed the fire with oblation and beat the rhythm at cool Parankundram, where Murugan of the drum is worshipped; then she mocks the oath again, saying she has caught the oath from his mouth that never lies to anyone, and the unit ends in obscure lines about a bull, a goad and the hanging bell struck by hand.
paripadal:8:72-89.nuance: The love quarrel turns into a vow of worship in the middle of a sentence (lines 78 to 82): the god at the hill is the one place where the wife's grief can be taken. ஒருவர்க்கும் பொய்யா நின் வாய் (line 84) is sarcasm. Lines 85 to 89 (எருமை இருத் தோட்டி, காளை, தூங்கு மணி) are not secure in sense or speaker.

thinai_evidence.note: the same husband-and-wife quarrel over the oath, now turned to the god

paripadal:8:90-111.reading: From the wind-beaten peaks the rain swells, the branches drip, the groves bloom, the pools fill with mud and the broad road is spread with marutham sand and flowers, and the small-footed women rise to join the festival; the worshippers carry sandal of many kinds, incense, lamps the wind cannot put out, fragrant flowers, drums, bells, ropes, peacocks, axes and the elephant image, and they ask their boons: some that what their hand touched in a dream should come true in waking, and that the Vaigai's flood adorn them, some vow that a child come to the womb, some whisper that their work for wealth succeed, some worship that their lord win in battle; the songs' rhythms, the dancers' beats on the stage and the thunder of the cloud-swept hill make a clamour that never sleeps.
paripadal:8:90-111.nuance: The petitions are this-worldly and specific (a lover seen in a dream, a child, wealth from work, a husband's victory), and each is matched to a ritual act: asking a boon, making a vow, speaking into the god's ear, offering worship. அரு வரைச் சேராத் தொழுநர் (line 102) may be worshippers who do not climb the hill and pray from its foot.

thinai_evidence.note: the festival crowd's offerings and petitions to the god, under paadaan

paripadal:8:112-130.reading: Girls rise after diving in the green pool, and their eyes, open faces, feet, golden ear ornaments, hands, budding breasts and red mouths are so like the lotus, water lily and the other flowers of the flowing water that the two cannot be told apart; the sharp-toothed women's breast ornaments meet the chests of men handsome as the god of love, the men give the women the nectar of joy as their right, and the women with bodies like red shoots ease the young men's longing; so lovers bound in marriage and those not yet together gather to honour the guarded town of the lord who dwells in the kadambu, and the poet prays that the wealth of streaming falls and springs, the gift of the god born to the dark-throated lord from the spotless lady, may last for cool Parankundram even when the sky dries up and the earth cracks.
paripadal:8:112-130.nuance: The bathing girls become the pool's flowers (புலம் வேறுபாடுறா, line 117), so the shrine's water is where love and worship join, and the closing prayer asks that this water, not the rain, be permanent. எம் கைப் பதுமம் (line 115) slips into a first-person voice. Lines 127 and 128 (மறு மிடற்று அண்ணற்கு மாசிலோள் தந்த) are read here as naming the god as the son Uma gave to Siva; they could also make the falls her gift.

words: கடம்பு அமர் செல்வன் கடி நகர் பேண
thinai_evidence.note: lovers' play at the pool ending in worship and a prayer for the hill: paadaan carrying akam matter

links.note: Paripadal 5.48-49 narrates the birth on a lotus bed in the green pool of the Himalaya; Paripadal 8.11-16 says Parankundram equals the Himalaya because its pool equals that pool of the lotus that bore him.
links.teaches: Read together, the birth story of song 5 becomes the title deed of song 8: the poet claims the Himalaya's sanctity for a Pandya hill by matching its pool to the birth pool, so the myth is used to found a local shrine.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 167 gives the attending gods as a sum (நால்வேறு இயற்கைப் பதினொரு மூவரொடு); Paripadal 8.4-7 names the same thirty-three group by group: twelve, two who speak of medicine, eight, and eleven from the lord of Aathirai.
links.teaches: The guide poem's 'eleven times three of four kinds' is spelled out in the Paripadal as four counted groups, showing that the Vedic thirty-three were known in Tamil by their divisions and that both poets made Murugan the one they attend.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the hill west of Koodal, with bees humming over pool flowers that open like eyes; Paripadal 8.17-28 makes the same bees, pools and flowers the god's procession, the coming from your hill to Koodal (குன்றத்தான் கூடல் வரவு).
links.teaches: The guide poem fixes Parankundram by its position beside the city, while the Paripadal turns the road between them into a seasonal procession of sound and bloom, so together they show the shrine defined by its tie to Madurai rather than as a lone mountain retreat.

links.note: In Natrinai 386 the girl refuses the hero's offer of a dread oath by the god (அணங்குடை அருஞ் சூள்) because men of his kin do not need it, and he comes with marriage; in Paripadal 8.65-71 the wife refuses her husband's oath by Murugan because the god's spear would devour a false swearer.
links.teaches: Both women stop a man from swearing by the god, but for opposite reasons, trust in his kin in the courtship poem and certainty of his guilt in the marriage quarrel, which shows that refusing the god-oath was a recognised move whose meaning depended on the stage of love.

links.note: In Akananuru 166 the husband soothes his wife by calling on the Velur god to afflict him if he went to the other woman, and the other woman exposes the lie; in Paripadal 8.65-66 the wife forbids such an oath by Murugan, since the god's true spear would eat him.
links.teaches: The Akananuru shows the god-oath used lightly as a husband's comfort, the Paripadal shows a wife who takes the same self-curse seriously enough to block it, so together they reveal that the oath was believed to bind the swearer bodily and that a knowing wife could protect a lying husband from it.

links.note: Kuruntokai 53 says the oath the man swore at the sandy ford with the hill goddesses as witness is what afflicts us, the women (எம்மணங் கினவே); Paripadal 8.66 says the god's spear will devour the man himself if he swears falsely.
links.teaches: On the plain reading of each, the two poems disagree on whom a broken god-witnessed oath strikes, the deceived women in the Kuruntokai and the perjurer in the Paripadal, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to where the god's punishment falls.

links.note: Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram; at Parankundram in Paripadal 8.103-108 the festival crowd asks for a dream lover made real, a child in the womb, success in making wealth (செய் பொருள் வாய்க்க) and victory in war.
links.teaches: The same collection holds a poet's refusal of worldly boons and a festival crowd's petitions for exactly those boons, so the Paripadal's devotion is not one ethic: the singer's ideal prayer and the people's practical vows stand side by side in it.

links.note: Paripadal 8.96-108 shows the crowd at Parankundram carrying flowers, incense and lamps and asking for children, wealth and victory; Thiruppugazh 8, sung at Parangiri, confesses that the poet never worshipped with flowers or walked round the hill and asks only that Murugan come at the hour of death.
links.teaches: The rites the Sangam festival performs as means to this-world ends become, at the same hill a thousand years later, the list of duties the devotee confesses he failed, and the request moves from children and wealth to rescue at death.

links.note: Kural 17 says even the great sea loses its nature if the cloud withholds rain; Paripadal 8.128-130 prays that the hill's streaming falls and springs last even when the sky dries and the earth cracks (மண் பரிய வானம் வறப்பினும், மன்னுகமா).
links.teaches: The Kural makes every water, the sea included, depend on rain, and the Paripadal asks that the god's waterfall be exempt from that law, which is what marks the shrine's water as sacred rather than natural.

source_issues: Paripadal 8: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan பாலையாழ் is a musical mode, not a thinai.
Paripadal 8 line 9 and line 52 have gaps (dots in the source), and line 1 has dashes after மண்மிசை (flags).
Paripadal 8 line 51: flagged as a line once taken for a modern heading; it reads as verse and the units count it (flag).
Paripadal 8 lines 23, 24, 48, 49, 73 and 74 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 8 line 117: lost vowel sign ொ restored in the -ஒடு fault (flag).
Paripadal 8 line 119: மாரண் is likely a misprint for மாரன்.
Paripadal 8 lines 85-89 are obscure in sense and speaker as the text stands.
